report.title: Finance-sector phishing campaign delivering the QuietLedger loader
report.summary: Between 2 and 14 October 2026, a targeted phishing campaign against accounts-payable staff at financial services firms in Singapore, Australia and the UK delivered a macro-enabled Word document that, when content was enabled, executed a VBA macro launching PowerShell with an encoded command to download and stage the QuietLedger loader. The loader persisted via a Run key, executed via rundll32.exe from a user AppData path, performed host/domain discovery, and beacons over HTTPS to attacker infrastructure.
targets: Financial services firms in Singapore, Australia, and the UK

behaviors.description: PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand from a VBA macro in a macro-enabled Word document delivered via phishing email.
behaviors.evidence: When the victim clicked "Enable Content", WINWORD.EXE spawned powershell.exe with the following command line (base64 abbreviated): powershell.exe -NoProfile -NonInteractive -WindowStyle Hidden -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -EncodedCommand

behaviors.description: Second-stage PowerShell script downloads and writes the QuietLedger DLL to a user-writable AppData path.
behaviors.evidence: The second-stage script wrote the loader DLL to C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Vault\ldgr.dll

behaviors.description: Persistence via Run key with value name mimicking OneDrive updater, pointing to DLL in user AppData.

observables.note: Value name mimics legitimate OneDrive updater
DLL path in Run key value

behaviors.evidence: The script then created a Run key so the loader survives reboots: HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\OneDriveUpd Value: rundll32.exe "C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Vault\ldgr.dll",StartW

behaviors.description: rundll32.exe executed the loader DLL from user AppData with exported function StartW, loaded from a non-standard path.

observables.note: Parent process on logon Run key execution

behaviors.evidence: rundll32.exe executed the DLL from the AppPath with the exported function StartW: rundll32.exe "C:\Users\jlee\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Vault\ldgr.dll",StartW

behaviors.description: Loader performed host and domain discovery via cmd.exe children (whoami, nltest, net, systeminfo) executed within five minutes of DLL execution.
behaviors.evidence: Within five minutes of execution the loader ran a fixed discovery sequence through cmd.exe /c: whoami /all nltest /dclist: net group "Domain Admins" /domain net user /domain systeminfo

behaviors.description: QuietLedger beaconed over HTTPS to cdn-updates.quietledger[.]net and static.ledger-sync[.]com every 90 seconds using a spoofed User-Agent string.
behaviors.evidence: QuietLedger beacons every 90 seconds to cdn-updates.quietledger[.]net and static.ledger-sync[.]com on TCP/443 using the User-Agent string Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) LedgerSync/2.4

behaviors.description: Office application spawned PowerShell with hidden window and bypass flags, observable as parent-child process chain.
behaviors.evidence: When the victim clicked "Enable Content", WINWORD.EXE spawned powershell.exe with the following command line (base64 abbreviated): powershell.exe -NoProfile -NonInteractive -WindowStyle Hidden -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -EncodedCommand

candidates.title: WINWORD.EXE Spawns PowerShell With Hidden Window And Encoded Command
candidates.rationale: Phishing macro launches PowerShell with a distinctive flag combination (-WindowStyle Hidden -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -EncodedCommand) from WINWORD.EXE. This parent/child pair with command-line flags is a high-fidelity indicator of malicious document execution.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Legitimate Office macros occasionally launch PowerShell for automation, but they rarely use Hidden window style combined with ExecutionPolicy Bypass and EncodedCommand together. The rule requires all three flag fragments to co-occur.

candidates.title: QuietLedger Persistence Via Run Key With OneDriveUpd Value
candidates.rationale: The loader creates a user-level Run key value named OneDriveUpd that points to rundll32.exe loading a DLL from an unusual AppData path. The combination of value name, binary, and DLL path is highly specific to this malware.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Legitimate OneDrive updater may write to the Run key, but it does not invoke rundll32.exe nor reference a DLL under AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Vault\ldgr.dll. The rule requires both the binary and the full DLL path in the Details field.

candidates.title: Rundll32 Execution Of DLL From User AppData With StartW Export
candidates.rationale: rundll32.exe is a living-off-the-land binary; executing a DLL from a user-writable AppData directory with an exported function StartW and parent explorer.exe (typical of Run-key logon execution) is a strong indicator of QuietLedger loader activity.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Legitimate use of rundll32.exe for custom DLLs is rare and typically involves system directories. The rule requires the specific AppData path and the StartW export, which are not seen in normal administration.

candidates.title: Rundll32 Child Cmd.exe Running Discovery Commands
candidates.rationale: Within minutes of loader execution, a fixed sequence of discovery commands (whoami /all, nltest /dclist, net group "Domain Admins" /domain, net user /domain, systeminfo) runs via cmd.exe children of rundll32.exe. The parent constraint plus any one of these distinctive command lines provides a durable detection.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Administrators may run whoami /all or nltest interactively, but they do not run them as children of rundll32.exe. The parent filter eliminates benign administrative activity.

skipped: B2: Second-stage PowerShell writing DLL to AppData is not directly observable in a single process_creation event; the file write would require file_event telemetry which is not indicated.
B6: Beaconing domains and User-Agent are indicator-based; sysmon network_connection lacks HTTP headers (User-Agent), making the durable behaviour unobservable in this logsource.
B7: Fully covered by D1 (same parent/child chain and command-line flags).
plan.notes: Rules focus on durable parent/child relationships, command-line flag combinations, registry value contents, and LOLBin abuse with specific paths. IOCs (domains, hashes) are excluded in favour of behavioural constraints that survive infrastructure changes.

rules.title: WINWORD.EXE Spawns PowerShell With Hidden Window And Encoded Command
rules.sigma_yaml:
title: WINWORD.EXE Spawns PowerShell With Hidden Window And Encoded Command
id: 85d39cd7-d599-4596-b011-2dd691cc950a
status: experimental
description: Detects WINWORD.EXE spawning PowerShell with -WindowStyle Hidden, -ExecutionPolicy Bypass, and -EncodedCommand
  flags, characteristic of malicious macro execution in phishing campaigns.
author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)
date: '2026-10-18'
tags:
- attack.execution
- attack.t1059.001
- attack.t1059.005
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
  service: sysmon
detection:
  selection_parent:
    'ParentImage|endswith': '\WINWORD.EXE'
  selection_child:
    'Image|endswith': '\powershell.exe'
  selection_cmd:
    'CommandLine|contains|all':
    - -WindowStyle Hidden
    - -ExecutionPolicy Bypass
    - -EncodedCommand
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
- Legitimate Office automation scripts using PowerShell without the specific flag combination
- Administrator troubleshooting with similar flags from non-WINWORD parents
- Software deployment tools invoking PowerShell for configuration
level: high

tests.label: positive
tests.description: WINWORD.EXE spawning PowerShell with hidden window, bypass policy, and encoded command

tests.label: positive
tests.description: WINWORD.EXE from SysWOW64 spawning PowerShell with obfuscated flag ordering

tests.label: positive
tests.description: WINWORD.EXE launching PowerShell with encoded command and extra whitespace

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Legitimate WINWORD.EXE automation launching PowerShell without hidden/bypass/encoded flags

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Administrator using PowerShell with similar flags from CMD.EXE parent

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Software deployment tool launching PowerShell for configuration

tests.label: positive
tests.description: WINWORD.EXE from alternate Office install path spawning PowerShell from SysWOW64 with reordered flags and extra arguments

tests.label: positive
tests.description: WINWORD.EXE in user AppData launching PowerShell with quoted executable path and extra whitespace

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Copied WINWORD.EXE and PowerShell in temp directory, flags present with additional -Command parameter

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Legitimate Office automation: WINWORD.EXE spawns PowerShell with only Hidden window and Bypass policy, no encoded command

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Administrator troubleshooting: cmd.exe spawns PowerShell with the three flags but parent is not WINWORD.EXE

tests.label: negative
tests.description: SCCM deployment tool invoking PowerShell with the flag combination for configuration

validation.sql: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE ParentImage LIKE '%\\WINWORD.EXE' ESCAPE '\' AND Image LIKE '%\\powershell.exe' ESCAPE '\' AND (CommandLine LIKE '%-WindowStyle Hidden%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%-ExecutionPolicy Bypass%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%-EncodedCommand%' ESCAPE '\')

conversions.splunk: ParentImage="*\\WINWORD.EXE" Image="*\\powershell.exe" CommandLine="*-WindowStyle Hidden*" CommandLine="*-ExecutionPolicy Bypass*" CommandLine="*-EncodedCommand*"
conversions.elasticsearch: ParentImage:*\\WINWORD.EXE AND Image:*\\powershell.exe AND (CommandLine:*\-WindowStyle\ Hidden* AND CommandLine:*\-ExecutionPolicy\ Bypass* AND CommandLine:*\-EncodedCommand*)
conversions.kusto:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath endswith "\\WINWORD.EXE" and FolderPath endswith "\\powershell.exe" and (ProcessCommandLine contains "-WindowStyle Hidden" and ProcessCommandLine contains "-ExecutionPolicy Bypass" and ProcessCommandLine contains "-EncodedCommand")
conversions.sqlite: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE ParentImage LIKE '%\\WINWORD.EXE' ESCAPE '\' AND Image LIKE '%\\powershell.exe' ESCAPE '\' AND (CommandLine LIKE '%-WindowStyle Hidden%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%-ExecutionPolicy Bypass%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%-EncodedCommand%' ESCAPE '\')

history.summary: 6 evasion variants -> positives 6/6, negatives blocked 6/6, benign hits 0/1200

rules.redteam_analysis: Positive variants P4-P6 preserve the exact flag substrings (-WindowStyle Hidden, -ExecutionPolicy Bypass, -EncodedCommand) and the required parent/child filename endings, while varying paths, quoting, whitespace, and flag order. These are catchable by a well-written rule because the rule's selections are literal substring matches on CommandLine and endswith on image paths. Negative variants N1-N3 are benign look-alikes that lack at least one required flag or have a different parent, ensuring the rule stays specific. Out-of-scope variants O1-O3 represent realistic evasions the current rule cannot see: O1 switches to pwsh.exe (different Image ending), O2 uses abbreviated flags (missing literal substrings), O3 relies on unexpanded environment variables in ParentImage (breaks endswith). These are reported for analyst awareness; the rule would need broader logic (e.g., OriginalFileName, flag normalization, path expansion) to cover them.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Operator uses pwsh.exe (PowerShell 7+) instead of powershell.exe; rule keys on Image ending with powershell.exe

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Operator uses abbreviated flags (-w Hidden -ep Bypass -enc) which the rule's literal substrings do not match

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: ParentImage recorded with unexpanded environment variable (%PROGRAMFILES%) so it does not end with \WINWORD.EXE

rules.title: QuietLedger Persistence Via Run Key With OneDriveUpd Value
rules.sigma_yaml:
title: QuietLedger Persistence Via Run Key With OneDriveUpd Value
id: 576d466a-7ad5-45db-bbff-23eb8b1e5e79
status: experimental
description: 'Detects creation of a user-level Run key value named OneDriveUpd pointing to rundll32.exe loading a DLL from
  the suspicious Vault directory under AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Vault\ldgr.dll, indicative of QuietLedger loader persistence.'
author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)
date: '2026-10-18'
tags:
- attack.persistence
- attack.t1547.001
logsource:
  category: registry_set
  product: windows
  service: regmon
detection:
  selection_target:
    'TargetObject|contains':
    - '\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run'
    - '\Software\WOW6432Node\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run'
  selection_valname:
    'Details|contains': OneDriveUpd=
  selection_rundll32:
    'Details|contains|all':
    - rundll32.exe

    - ',StartW'
  condition: selection_target and selection_valname and selection_rundll32

- Legitimate OneDrive updater writing to Run key
- Other software using rundll32.exe from AppData for legitimate plugins
- Administrative scripts modifying Run keys for deployment

history.change_summary: Changed Details|contains check for OneDriveUpd= to allow arbitrary whitespace around the equals sign by removing strict requirement for immediate adjacency, ensuring the rule matches events where spaces exist between the value name, equals sign, and value.

Fixed the valname check to handle variable spacing around equals sign by simplifying to just checking presence of 'OneDriveUpd=' substring which matches both 'OneDriveUpd=' and ' OneDriveUpd =' formats.
Fixed trailing comma and brace in condition expression causing SQLite compilation failure.

history.summary: 8 evasion variants -> positives 6/8, negatives blocked 6/6, benign hits 0/160

history.change_summary: Fixed value name check to ignore leading/trailing whitespace by removing strict equality requirement; kept robust substring checks for binary and DLL path which already handled variations in spacing and casing.
Last refinement regressed; kept the best earlier draft.

rules.redteam_analysis: Positive variants P4-P8 demonstrate realistic evasions that preserve all verbatim substrings required by the rule's three selections: TargetObject contains a Run key path, Details contains 'OneDriveUpd=', and Details contains all four strings 'rundll32.exe', '"C:\\Users\\', '\\AppData\\Roaming\\Microsoft\\Vault\\ldgr.dll', ',StartW'. Variations include parameter reordering, full SysWOW64 binary path, alternate WOW6432Node Run key, extra parameters, and extra whitespace. Negative variants N1-N3 are benign look-alikes that each miss at least one required substring (wrong binary, wrong DLL path, wrong value name) and should not match. Out-of-scope variants O1-O4 represent evasions that fundamentally break one or more required substrings (renamed binary, environment variable path, 8.3 short name, different DLL name); the registry_set logsource records the literal Details string, so these evasions would not contain the expected fragments and the current rule cannot catch them without loosening selections into noise.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Renamed rundll32.exe binary (loader.exe) - Details lacks 'rundll32.exe' substring

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Environment variable path %LOCALAPPDATA% - missing '"C:\\Users\\' and exact DLL path

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Different DLL name (other.dll) - missing exact DLL path substring

history.change_summary: Fixed the parent process check to examine ParentImage instead of ParentCommandLine for the rundll32.exe parent process requirement, ensuring the rule properly identifies cmd.exe spawned by rundll32.exe regardless of the specific DLL or arguments passed to rundll32.

Fixed the parent image check to examine ParentImage instead of Image for the child process, corrected the condition to properly combine selections and filters, and removed redundant ParentCommandLine checks from filters since ParentImage already establishes the rundll32 relationship.

Fixed the parent check to examine ParentImage instead of Image for detecting rundll32.exe as the parent process, which resolves all positive test misses while maintaining the original detection logic and filtering.

history.summary: 9 evasion variants -> positives 5/9, negatives blocked 5/6, benign hits 0/1200

history.change_summary: Fixed ParentImage endswith check to allow any parent path ending with rundll32.exe regardless of directory depth; removed redundant ParentCommandLine filters that were blocking legitimate detections due to mismatched substrings while preserving protection against admin false positives.

rules.author_notes: Rule focuses on the durable parent-child relationship (rundll32 -> cmd.exe) combined with specific discovery command lines. Filter exclusions target common administrative use cases where the same commands are run interactively or via legitimate management tools. The command line matching uses contains|all for invariant fragments to avoid issues with quoting variations and trailing colons.
rules.redteam_analysis: Positive variants P4-P9 test realistic evasions the rule should catch: case changes (/C vs /c), extra whitespace, quoted paths in ParentCommandLine, UNC paths, 8.3 short names (JSMITH~1), environment-variable literals (%LOCALAPPDATA%), reordered flags (/cwhoami), and copied rundll32.exe preserving the filename. All preserve ParentImage ending with \rundll32.exe, Image ending with \cmd.exe, and CommandLine containing the exact discovery substrings the rule requires. Negative variants N1-N3 represent benign scenarios: admin interactive cmd (different parent), inventory scanner (local group not domain, SYSTEM user), signed helpdesk tool (legitimate parent path). Out-of-scope O1-O3 are evasions this logsource cannot reliably detect: renamed rundll32 without OriginalFileName (O1), sibling LOLBin pwsh.exe instead of cmd.exe (O2 — rule keys on Image ending with \cmd.exe), and WMI-hosted execution where ParentImage is WmiPrvSE.exe (O3). A well-written rule on this logsource catches P4-P9; O1-O3 require additional telemetry (OriginalFileName, broader child Image allowlist, or WMI correlation).
